growth_story.headline: Armenia's income per person went from collapse to boom, bust and boom again; inflows from Russia since 2022 helped carry it to a new peak in 2025.
growth_story.arc: Income per person fell hard after independence, by 41.1 percent in 1992 alone, and the 1991–2000 era averaged -1.5 percent a year; the sources say little about the causes of that slump. From 2001 to 2008 growth averaged 12.5 percent, driven mainly by a building boom paid for largely by money that migrants, most of them in Russia, sent home. When the global crisis cut those remittances, exports and foreign investment, income per person fell 13.5 percent in 2009, and a second shock from Russia in 2014–15 held the 2009–2016 era to 1.7 percent. Growth picked up to 5.5 percent in 2017–2025, despite a fall of 7.2 percent in 2020, and jumped 12.3 percent in 2022 as foreign currency, migrants and firms moved in from Russia after its war in Ukraine began. Income per person reached its highest level so far in 2025, while the IMF describes those exceptional drivers as gradually tapering off.

threads.title: Remittances built the 2000s boom
threads.text: In the 2001–2008 era, money sent home by migrants paid for a building boom, and construction grew very fast. When remittances fell in 2009, construction output dropped sharply, and income per person fell 13.5 percent that year.

threads.title: Two shocks from Russia
threads.text: Most remittances come from Russia, so swings in Russia's economy reach Armenia directly. After the 2009 crisis, falling oil prices and sanctions on Russia hit Armenia again in 2014–15. The World Bank judged in 2017 that the model behind the earlier boom was exhausted, and the 2009–2016 era averaged 1.7 percent.

threads.title: Inflows after Russia's war
threads.text: From 2022, foreign currency, migrants and businesses arrived from Russia, and income per person grew 12.3 percent that year and 8.5 percent in 2023. The IMF calls these drivers exceptional and says they are gradually tapering off; income per person grew 3.5 percent in 2024 and 5.4 percent in 2025.

threads.title: Closed borders, new routes
threads.text: Armenia is landlocked, and its borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey have long been closed, which raises the cost of trade. A peace agreement with Azerbaijan was initialed in August 2025, and the World Bank now counts its finalization, along with continued progress on TRIPP, among the things that could add to growth.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank's 2017 diagnostic calls Armenia an important success story among transition economies from independence in 1991 until the 2008–09 crisis. The data show a deep fall first: income per person dropped 41.1 percent in 1992, the 1991–2000 era averaged -1.5 percent, and income per person did not pass its 1990 level again until 2003.
